title: Resume Writing Fundamentals for Internship Applicants
body:
Recruiters at large employers often spend less than a minute on a first pass through a resume, so your resume has one job: make it easy to see that you can do the work. For undergraduate internship applicants, keep the resume to one page. A second page almost always means you are including material that is not relevant to the role.

Start with your name, a professional email address, a phone number, a city and state, and a link to LinkedIn or a portfolio if you have one. Do not include a photo, your date of birth, marital status, or a full street address. U.S. employers do not expect them, and they invite bias.

List education first while you are a student: school, degree, major, expected graduation month and year, and GPA if it is 3.0 or higher. Relevant coursework can be a single line, but only list courses that match the posting.

The experience section carries most of the weight. Write each bullet as action plus result: begin with a strong verb, describe what you did, and quantify the outcome whenever you can. Compare "Responsible for social media" with "Grew the club's Instagram following from 300 to 1,150 in one semester by launching a weekly student-spotlight series." The second bullet shows scope, initiative, and impact. Class projects, research, hackathons, and part-time jobs all count as experience; describe them with the same action-plus-result structure.

Many employers use an applicant tracking system (ATS) that parses your resume into fields. Use a simple single-column layout, standard section headings such as Education, Experience, Projects, and Skills, and a common font. Avoid tables, text boxes, and graphics for essential information because some systems cannot read them. Mirror the exact language of the posting when it is true for you: if the posting asks for SQL and Tableau and you have used both, name them exactly.

Finally, tailor your resume for each application. Reorder bullets so the most relevant experience appears first, and save the file as a PDF named with your first and last name.

title: Resumes and CVs for Graduate and Research Students
body:
Graduate students face a different resume question than undergraduates: how much of your research, teaching, and publication record belongs on an industry internship application? The answer depends on the role.

For industry internships in data science, machine learning, research engineering, or quantitative roles, a master's or PhD student with substantial research may use a two-page resume. The second page is justified when it contains publications, conference presentations, or research projects that directly match the role. If your second page only holds coursework and older jobs, cut back to one page. Note that this guidance intentionally differs from the one-page rule for undergraduates; reviewers of research-heavy roles expect to see evidence of research depth.

An academic curriculum vitae (CV) is not the same document. A CV lists everything: every publication, every talk, teaching appointments, service, and grants, and it can run many pages. Use a CV for academic positions, fellowships, and some government research labs. Use a resume for industry internships, even research internships, unless the posting explicitly asks for a CV.

When converting research into resume bullets, translate academic language into business outcomes. Instead of "Investigated heterogeneous treatment effects in observational panel data," write "Built a causal-inference model in Python that estimated which customer segments responded to a price change, reducing the estimation error by 18 percent compared with the baseline approach." Name the methods and tools an industry reviewer will search for, such as Python, PyTorch, SQL, causal inference, or A/B testing.

Include a Publications section only if you have published or have papers under review, and use a consistent citation format with your name in bold. Put teaching assistant roles under Experience and describe them in terms of communication and leadership, for example "Led weekly lab sections for 45 students and redesigned two assignments that cut average grading questions by half."

International graduate students should not list visa status on the resume. Work authorization is discussed later in the process, and the application form will usually ask about it directly.

title: Behavioral Interviews and the STAR Method
body:
Behavioral interview questions ask you to describe how you handled real situations in the past, on the theory that past behavior predicts future behavior. Typical questions include "Tell me about a time you worked with a difficult teammate," "Describe a time you failed," and "Give an example of when you took initiative."

The STAR method gives your answer a clear structure. Situation: set the scene in one or two sentences. Task: explain what you were responsible for. Action: describe the specific steps you personally took; this should be the longest part of your answer. Result: share the outcome, with numbers if possible, and what you learned. A strong STAR answer takes about one and a half to two minutes to deliver.

Use "I" rather than "we" when describing actions. Interviewers want to know what you did, not what the team did. If the result was not a success, that is acceptable; describe what you learned and what you would do differently. Failure stories are often memorable precisely because they show self-awareness.

Prepare a story bank before interview season. Write down six to eight experiences from classes, jobs, clubs, volunteer work, or projects, and map each one to common themes: leadership, conflict, failure, ambiguity, tight deadlines, persuading others, and learning a new skill quickly. Most stories can answer two or three different questions if you shift the emphasis.

Practice out loud, not just in your head. Record yourself answering three questions and watch the recording: check whether you rambled through the situation, skipped the result, or used filler words. Practice with a friend or schedule a mock interview with a career advisor.

Common mistakes include giving hypothetical answers ("I would...") instead of real examples, choosing a story where you were not the main actor, speaking negatively about former teammates or managers, and forgetting to state the result. End each answer by connecting what you learned to the role you are interviewing for, which shows that you have thought about the job and not just about yourself.

title: Preparing for Technical Interviews: Coding, SQL, and Case Questions
body:
Technical interviews test whether you can reason through a problem in your field, not whether you have memorized answers. The format depends on the role.

Software engineering internships usually include one or two coding interviews. You will solve a problem involving arrays, strings, hash maps, trees, or graphs, either in a shared online editor or on a whiteboard. Interviewers care about your process: restate the problem, ask clarifying questions about inputs and edge cases, describe a simple approach first, then improve it. Talk through your thinking continuously, because silence makes it impossible for the interviewer to give you credit or hints. Analyze time and space complexity at the end, and test your code with a small example. Practice twenty to forty problems across common patterns rather than hundreds of random problems.

Data analyst and data science interviews often include a SQL exercise. Expect questions that require joins, GROUP BY with aggregation, filtering with HAVING, window functions such as ROW_NUMBER and LAG, and handling of NULL values. Read the table schema carefully and say aloud what each table represents before writing a query. Some interviews add a statistics question about A/B tests, p-values, or sampling bias, or a take-home assignment analyzing a dataset.

Product management, consulting, and business analyst interviews often use case questions. You may be asked to estimate a market size, diagnose why a metric dropped, or design a feature. Structure your answer before diving in, state assumptions explicitly, and do arithmetic out loud. For a metric drop, separate internal causes such as a product change or bug from external causes such as seasonality or a competitor, and check data quality first.

Design roles typically include a portfolio review in which you walk through one or two projects, explaining the problem, your research, alternatives you rejected, and the outcome.

For every technical interview, it is acceptable to say "I am not sure, but here is how I would find out." Honest reasoning earns more credit than a confident wrong answer. Ask your interviewer a thoughtful question at the end about how the team works.

title: Networking and Informational Interviews
body:
Networking is not asking strangers for jobs. It is building relationships with people who can teach you about a field, a company, or a role, and who may later recommend you. Many internships are filled faster when a current employee refers a candidate, so relationships matter.

Start with people who are easiest to reach: alumni from your university, former classmates who are now working, professors' former students, and speakers who visit your clubs. LinkedIn's alumni tool lets you filter graduates of your school by company and job title.

An informational interview is a twenty-minute conversation in which you ask someone about their work. It is not a job interview, and you should not ask for a job or a referral during the first conversation. Send a short message: introduce yourself in one sentence, explain the specific reason you are reaching out to this person, and ask for fifteen or twenty minutes at their convenience. For example: "Hi Jordan, I'm a junior studying information systems at the university, and I saw you moved from consulting into product analytics. I'm exploring that path and would love to hear how you made the switch. Would you have 20 minutes in the next few weeks?"

Prepare five or six questions: what a typical week looks like, what skills matter most, what surprised them about the role, how they would prepare if they were a student today, and who else they recommend you talk to. The last question is the most valuable because it grows your network.

Send a thank-you note within twenty-four hours that mentions one specific piece of advice you plan to act on. Then follow up a few weeks later to report what you did with that advice. This follow-up is what turns a single conversation into a relationship.

Keep a simple spreadsheet of the people you have talked to, the date, what you discussed, and when to follow up. If someone later offers to refer you, make it easy: send the job link, your resume, and two sentences about why you fit the role.

title: Evaluating and Comparing Internship Offers
body:
Receiving more than one internship offer is a good problem, but choosing well requires looking beyond the hourly rate. Compare offers on five dimensions.

First, the work itself. Ask what project you will own, whether it will ship or be used, and what a successful intern accomplished last year. An internship with a real project and a clear deliverable usually teaches more than one with a famous name and vague tasks.

Second, mentorship. Ask who your manager will be, how often you will meet, and whether you will have a separate mentor or buddy. Weekly one-on-ones and regular feedback are signs of a well-run program.

Third, total compensation and cost. Compare the hourly rate multiplied by expected hours, plus any housing stipend, relocation assistance, or transit benefits, minus the cost of living in that city. A $40/hour internship in a city with very high rent can leave you with less money than a $28/hour remote role.

Fourth, conversion potential. Ask what percentage of interns received return offers last year. Large companies often hire most full-time entry-level employees from their intern pool.

Fifth, logistics and fit: start date, remote or onsite expectations, team culture, and, for international students, whether the employer supports the work authorization you need.

Unpaid internships deserve extra scrutiny. In the United States, the Department of Labor uses a "primary beneficiary" test for for-profit employers: an unpaid internship should mainly benefit the intern, typically through training tied to an academic program, rather than providing free labor. Academic credit alone does not make an internship fair. If an unpaid role asks you to do the same work as paid staff, discuss it with your career center before accepting.

Many offers include a response deadline. If you need more time because you are waiting on another company, it is professional to ask politely for an extension, explain the reason honestly, and propose a specific date. Avoid accepting an offer and later reneging; it can damage your reputation with the employer and with your university's relationship with that employer.

title: Negotiating an Internship Offer
body:
Students often assume internship offers cannot be negotiated. At many large companies, intern pay is fixed for the entire cohort and will not change, but other parts of the offer often can. At startups and smaller companies, the hourly rate itself may be flexible.

Before negotiating, research the market. Look at what similar roles in the same city pay using your career center's salary survey, offers your classmates have shared, and published intern salary data. Know your own priorities: is it pay, start date, remote flexibility, housing, or the team you join?

The items most commonly negotiated for internships are the start and end dates, the team or project placement, relocation or housing support, remote days, and the response deadline. Pay is sometimes negotiable when you hold a competing offer at a higher rate.

Negotiate with enthusiasm and specifics. A good script is: "I'm very excited about this offer and the analytics team. I have another offer at $32 an hour with a similar scope. Is there any flexibility to get closer to that rate? If not, I would still love to discuss a housing stipend, since I'll be relocating." Be honest. Never invent a competing offer; recruiters talk to each other, and getting caught can end the process.

Ask once, clearly, and then accept the answer gracefully. If the company says the rate is fixed for all interns, thank them and ask whether any other part of the package has flexibility. Then make your decision.

Get any agreed changes in writing, ideally an updated offer letter or at least an email confirmation from the recruiter.

If you are deciding between offers, negotiation is also a way to gather information. How a company responds to a respectful request tells you something about how it treats its people. A recruiter who responds with pressure or threats is giving you useful data about the culture.

Finally, do not negotiate after you have already accepted an offer. Once you accept, the terms are agreed, and reopening them damages trust.

title: Internship Etiquette and Your First 30 Days
body:
The first month of an internship sets the impression that your manager will remember when they decide on a return offer. Most of what matters is professionalism rather than technical brilliance.

In your first week, meet with your manager to agree on what success looks like by the end of the internship. Write it down and confirm it by email. Ask how your manager prefers to communicate: chat for quick questions, email for updates, or a scheduled weekly meeting. Learn the names and roles of the people on your team and the people your project depends on.

Ask questions, but ask good ones. Spend about fifteen to thirty minutes trying to solve a problem on your own first, then ask, explaining what you already tried. This shows initiative and respects other people's time. Keep a running document of answers so you never ask the same question twice.

Send a short written update at the end of each week: what you completed, what you are working on next, and anything blocking you. Managers are busy, and a weekly update makes your progress visible without requiring a meeting.

Be reliable about time. Arrive on time for meetings, respond to messages within the same business day, and tell your manager in advance if you will be absent. In remote internships, keep your camera on in team meetings unless the team norm is otherwise, and update your status so people know when you are available.

Treat confidential information carefully. Do not post about internal projects on social media, and ask before sharing any work in your portfolio after the internship ends. Many companies require written permission.

Finally, build relationships beyond your team. Ask two or three people from other departments for a twenty-minute coffee chat about their work. These conversations help you understand the business and often become valuable professional connections after the internship ends. In the last week, thank your manager and mentor in writing and ask for honest feedback on what you should improve.

title: Cover Letters That Get Read
body:
Not every application requires a cover letter, but when one is requested or optional, a strong letter can set you apart, especially when your resume alone does not explain why you want this particular role. A cover letter should make one argument: here is why I am a strong fit for this specific job at this specific company.

Keep it to three or four short paragraphs and under one page, roughly 250 to 350 words. Address it to a named person if you can find the hiring manager or recruiter; otherwise, "Dear Hiring Team" is acceptable.

In the opening paragraph, name the role and give a specific reason you are interested in this company. Generic openings such as "I am writing to apply for the position" waste the reader's attention. Instead, connect to something real: a product you use, a project the company published, or a conversation with an employee.

In the middle paragraph or two, pick two requirements from the posting and prove you meet them with brief stories from your experience. Use the same action-and-result structure as your resume, but add context the resume cannot hold, such as why you made a decision or what you learned. Do not repeat your resume line by line.

In the closing paragraph, restate your interest, mention your availability, and thank the reader. Keep the tone confident but not arrogant.

Tailor every letter. Recruiters can recognize a template in seconds, especially when the letter names the wrong company, which happens more often than you might think. Before sending, check the company name, role title, and the hiring manager's name twice.

If you use an AI writing tool to draft a cover letter, treat the output as a rough draft. Replace generic phrases with your own specific experiences and make sure every claim is true. Employers increasingly recognize generic AI-generated letters, and a letter that does not sound like you can hurt more than having no letter at all.

Save the letter as a PDF and match its header and font to your resume so the two documents look like a set.

title: Work Authorization Basics for International Students (CPT, OPT, STEM OPT)
disclaimer: SIMPLIFIED COURSE MATERIAL - NOT LEGAL GUIDANCE. Immigration rules change and individual situations differ. Always confirm your options with your university's international student office (Designated School Official) or a qualified immigration attorney.
body:
This article is simplified course material for the CareerCompass demo and is not real legal guidance. International students on F-1 status need specific authorization before working in the United States, including for unpaid internships. The two most common options for internships are CPT and OPT.

Curricular Practical Training (CPT) allows F-1 students to work in an internship that is an integral part of their curriculum, for example a required internship course or a course that grants credit for the work. CPT is authorized by your school's Designated School Official, not by a government application, and it is tied to a specific employer and specific dates. Many schools require you to complete one full academic year before you are eligible, although some graduate programs allow CPT earlier. You need a job offer before you apply for CPT, and you may not begin working until the authorization appears on your updated Form I-20.

Optional Practical Training (OPT) provides up to twelve months of work authorization related to your field of study. It can be used during your studies (pre-completion OPT) or after graduation (post-completion OPT). OPT requires an application to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and an approved Employment Authorization Document before you start work, and processing can take several months, so plan ahead. Time used for pre-completion OPT is subtracted from the twelve months available after graduation.

Students with degrees in eligible STEM fields may apply for a STEM OPT extension of up to twenty-four additional months. The employer must participate in E-Verify and complete a training plan with you.

When a posting says an employer "does not sponsor visas," it often refers to long-term work visas such as the H-1B, not necessarily to CPT or OPT. If you are unsure, ask the recruiter directly and politely whether the role is open to students on CPT or OPT. Do not list your visa status on your resume; answer the question when the application asks.

Keep copies of every authorization document, track your dates carefully, and talk with your international student office before accepting any offer.

title: Career Fair Playbook (2026 Update)
body:
Our fall and spring career fairs are held in person in the Student Union ballroom, with more than one hundred and fifty employers attending each fair. A small number of employers also join a separate virtual session the following week for students who cannot attend in person.

Preparation starts a week before the fair. Review the employer list on CareerCompass, choose eight to twelve priority employers, and read one open posting from each. Group them into tiers: three or four top choices and the rest as practice. Visit a practice employer first to warm up before approaching your top choices.

Prepare a thirty-second introduction: your name, year, and major; one or two relevant experiences; and the type of role you are seeking at that company. For example: "Hi, I'm a junior in business analytics. This summer I built a Tableau dashboard that cut my campus job's weekly reporting time in half, and I'm looking for a data analyst internship. I read about your demand forecasting team and wanted to learn more." End with a question about the company, not a request for a job.

Bring printed copies of your resume, about fifteen, in a folder, even though many employers will also ask you to apply online. Dress in business casual unless the fair says otherwise. Bring a small notebook or use your phone to write down each recruiter's name and one detail from the conversation immediately after you walk away.

At each booth, make eye contact, introduce yourself, and listen more than you talk. Ask how their interns spend their time and what makes an applicant stand out. If the recruiter tells you to apply online, ask whether there is a specific requisition number to use and whether you may mention your conversation in the application.

Within twenty-four hours, send a short thank-you message on LinkedIn or by email to each recruiter you spoke with, referencing the detail you wrote down, and complete the online applications the same week. Employers often review fair applicants first, so speed matters.

title: Virtual Career Fair Guide (2021 Edition)
disclaimer: ARCHIVED - this guide was written for the 2021 virtual-only fairs and may be out of date. See the 2026 Career Fair Playbook.
body:
Because of public health restrictions, all of our career fairs are held entirely online this year through a video platform. There will be no in-person fair, and students should not come to the Student Union. Employers will host group information sessions and short one-on-one video chats that you reserve in advance.

Registration opens two weeks before each fair. Popular employers fill their one-on-one slots within hours, so log in as soon as registration opens and book your top choices immediately. You can usually book up to six one-on-one sessions and unlimited group sessions.

Test your technology the day before. Make sure your camera, microphone, and internet connection work, and close other applications that might slow down your computer. Use a laptop rather than a phone if possible. Choose a quiet, well-lit space with a plain background, and position the camera at eye level.

You do not need printed resumes. Instead, upload your resume as a PDF to your fair profile so recruiters can view it before your session. Make sure your profile includes a short headline describing the kind of role you want.

One-on-one sessions typically last ten minutes. Prepare a brief introduction of about thirty seconds and two or three questions about the company. Because time is short and video conversations can feel awkward, practice your introduction on a video call with a friend.

Dress professionally from head to toe, even though recruiters will only see you from the shoulders up, because it helps you feel prepared and avoids surprises if you need to stand.

After each session, send a thank-you message through the platform's chat feature or by email within twenty-four hours. Mention one detail from your conversation and confirm that you have applied online.

Virtual fairs make it easier to meet employers from other cities who would not normally travel to campus, so take advantage of the opportunity by including a few employers outside your home region.

title: Turning Your Internship into a Return Offer
body:
For many students, the most valuable outcome of an internship is a full-time return offer. Many employers fill a large share of their entry-level positions with former interns, so the internship works like an extended interview.

Understand how the decision is made. At most companies, your manager writes an evaluation near the end of the internship, often with input from your mentor and teammates, and a committee or senior leader approves offers. Ask your manager early, ideally in the first two weeks, how return offers are decided and what distinguished interns who received them in past years.

Deliver your project, and make its impact visible. Managers remember interns who finished what they started and could explain why it mattered. Keep a log of your accomplishments with numbers, such as hours saved, errors reduced, or users reached, so you can describe them clearly in your final presentation and your evaluation conversation.

Ask for feedback at the midpoint. A mid-internship check-in gives you time to correct course. Ask directly: "If my internship ended today, would I be on track for a return offer? What should I do differently in the second half?" Most managers appreciate the question and give more honest answers than students expect.

Your final presentation matters. Practice it, keep it to the time limit, start with the business problem and result, and leave time for questions. Invite the people who helped you.

Build relationships across the team, not only with your manager. Teammates' informal opinions influence the evaluation. Be someone people enjoy working with: reliable, curious, and generous with credit.

If you receive a return offer, you may have a deadline weeks or months before you graduate. Read the earlier guide on evaluating and comparing offers before deciding. If you do not receive an offer, ask politely for feedback, stay in touch with your manager, and ask whether they would serve as a reference. A strong reference from an internship is valuable even without an offer.

title: Building a Portfolio for Data, Design, and Software Roles
body:
A portfolio shows employers what you can do instead of telling them. For design roles it is usually required; for data and software roles it is a strong advantage, especially if you do not yet have internship experience.

Quality matters more than quantity. Two or three well-documented projects are better than ten unfinished ones. Each project should answer four questions: what problem you were solving and for whom, what you did and why you made the choices you made, what the result was, and what you would do differently next time.

For design portfolios, show your process, not only polished final screens. Include research findings, early sketches, alternatives you rejected, and usability test results. Reviewers want to see how you think. Host the portfolio on a simple personal website and make sure it loads quickly on a phone.

For data portfolios, choose datasets that connect to a real question rather than the same tutorial datasets everyone uses. Publish your analysis as a clean notebook or a short write-up with charts, and lead with the conclusion in plain language before showing the code. A dashboard that a non-technical person can understand is a powerful portfolio piece for analyst roles.

For software portfolios, put your code on GitHub with a clear README that explains what the project does, how to run it, and what you learned. Include screenshots or a short demo video. Recruiters rarely read the code itself, but engineers in later interview rounds may, so keep it readable and remove secrets such as API keys from the history.

Class projects count, as long as you describe your individual contribution honestly in group work. Never present a teammate's work as your own, and do not publish projects that contain confidential employer data or real people's personal information. If an assignment is reused each semester, ask your instructor before publishing your solution.

Link your portfolio from your resume, LinkedIn profile, and email signature, and update it after every major project.
